title: Consultancy Robustness to a Lying Consultant Across Model Scales
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped study of how consultant-judge capability gap affects deception success in scalable oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Consultancy Robustness to a Lying Consultant Across Model Scales

**Problem:** In consultancy, a single expert argues for one answer; a key risk is a consultant assigned to argue for the WRONG answer persuading the judge. How this persuasion success scales with the GAP between consultant and judge capability is not finely mapped.

**Direction:** Hold the judge fixed (small open model) and vary the consultant across a model-size ladder (0.5B, 1.5B, 7B). For each, measure how often a deliberately-wrong consultant flips the judge to the wrong answer. Plot 'deception success rate' vs consultant-judge capability gap.

**Why it matters:** If a more capable consultant deceives weak judges MORE effectively, naive scaling makes oversight worse — a crucial scaling-law-for-oversight question. Cheap inference-only experiment producing a clean dose-response curve.

**Relevant context:** Kenton et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.04622) found stronger debaters help judges, but consultancy is the weaker protocol; 'Scaling Laws for Scalable Oversight' (arXiv:2504.18530) motivates capability-gap framing.

title: Cross-Lingual Weak Judges: Oversight When Judge Reads a Second Language
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses a scalable-oversight gap (multilingual judge degradation) with a reasonably scoped approach.

original_idea.body:
# Cross-Lingual Weak Judges: Oversight When Judge Reads a Second Language

**Problem:** All major debate/judge experiments are English-only. A realistic future overseer may evaluate arguments in a language they (or their model) handle weakly. The degradation of oversight quality under a language-handicapped judge is unmeasured.

**Direction:** Translate a slice of QuALITY questions and debate transcripts into a lower-resource language. Use a small multilingual open model as judge in English vs the translated language. Measure how much judge accuracy in debate drops when the judge operates in its weaker language, and whether debate's lift over consultancy survives.

**Why it matters:** Multilingual oversight is a real-world deployment gap that no single lab prioritizes. Showing oversight protocols degrade in non-English regimes is valuable diffuse-evaluation work, fully inference-based.

**Relevant context:** Debate/consultancy benchmarks (Kenton 2024, Khan 2024) are English-only on QuALITY. Multilingual safety gaps are documented broadly but not for oversight protocols.

title: Time-Pressure Variation: How Judge Accuracy Degrades Under Token/Turn Budgets
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted study of resource-bounded oversight reliability, a recognized AI safety concern.

original_idea.body:
# Time-Pressure Variation: How Judge Accuracy Degrades Under Token/Turn Budgets

**Problem:** Prover-verifier work used TIME-CONSTRAINED humans. The analogous variable for LLM judges — a constrained reasoning budget (max tokens / turns the judge may use) — is rarely varied, yet real oversight is resource-bounded.

**Direction:** In a debate-judging setup with a small open model, cap the judge's allowed reasoning: zero-CoT, short-CoT (50 tokens), long-CoT (500 tokens). Measure judge accuracy and bias susceptibility (e.g., to verbosity/position) as a function of reasoning budget, across easy and hard questions.

**Why it matters:** Resource-bounded oversight is the realistic regime; knowing how thin a judge's reasoning budget can get before accuracy collapses guides protocol cost/benefit. Pure inference, easy to scope to 30h.

**Relevant context:** Kirchner et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.13692) used time-constrained human verifiers. LLM reasoning-budget effects on judging are underexplored in oversight contexts.

title: Does the Order of Debate Rounds Change Who Wins? Recency vs Primacy in Oversight
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped isolation of an exploitable order-bias vulnerability in debate oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Does the Order of Debate Rounds Change Who Wins? Recency vs Primacy in Oversight

**Problem:** Position bias is known for pairwise judging, but multi-turn debate has a temporal analogue: does the debater who speaks LAST (recency) or FIRST (primacy) gain an unfair edge with weak judges? This is rarely isolated in debate experiments.

**Direction:** Generate two-turn debate transcripts, then create variants where the SAME arguments are reordered (correct-side-first vs incorrect-side-first vs interleaved). Hold content fixed, vary only order. Measure how the weak judge's verdict shifts with ordering to quantify a recency/primacy oversight vulnerability.

**Why it matters:** If verdict depends on speaking order rather than argument merit, debate is exploitable by a model that games turn structure. A clean controlled variation isolating order from content, inference-only.

**Relevant context:** Position bias documented for pairwise LLM judging (GPT-4 ~10% first-position preference, arXiv:2410.02736). Debate's turn-order analogue is under-tested.

title: Critique-Then-Judge: Does an AI Critique Step Improve Weak-Judge Accuracy?
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted test of composing oversight mechanisms to improve weak-judge accuracy.

original_idea.body:
# Critique-Then-Judge: Does an AI Critique Step Improve Weak-Judge Accuracy?

**Problem:** CriticGPT helped humans review code; debate helps weak judges. An untested combination: inserting an automated CRITIQUE of each debater's argument before the judge decides. Whether critique-assistance stacks with debate, or is redundant, is unknown.

**Direction:** On QuALITY debate transcripts, add a stage where a small open critic model writes a bulleted list of weaknesses in each debater's argument; the weak judge then decides WITH vs WITHOUT the critique. Measure the accuracy delta from adding the critique layer, and whether it helps more on hard questions.

**Why it matters:** Composing oversight mechanisms (debate + critique) is a natural path to stronger protocols, and testing whether they're complementary or redundant is cheap and informative. Inference-only, public dataset.

**Relevant context:** CriticGPT (arXiv:2407.00215): AI critiques help humans catch more bugs. Debate (arXiv:2402.06782) helps judges. Their composition is unstudied.

title: Sycophancy Under Oversight: Does a Judge's Stated Preference Corrupt a Consultant?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped reward-hacking-of-oversight failure mode via sycophantic capitulation.

original_idea.body:
# Sycophancy Under Oversight: Does a Judge's Stated Preference Corrupt a Consultant?

**Problem:** Sycophancy makes models echo a user's stated belief. In interactive consultancy/debate, the judge asks questions — if the judge reveals a leaning, a sycophantic consultant may abandon a correct argument to agree. This feedback loop is not isolated in oversight setups.

**Direction:** Run interactive consultancy where the small-model judge's clarifying questions are scripted to either reveal a leaning toward the WRONG answer or stay neutral. Measure how often the consultant (arguing correctly) caves and switches to support the judge's revealed wrong leaning, comparing neutral vs leaning conditions.

**Why it matters:** If interactivity lets a biased overseer induce sycophantic capitulation, interactive oversight protocols are self-undermining — a subtle reward-hacking-of-oversight failure. Inference-only, directly on the open-problem list.

**Relevant context:** Sycophancy in LLMs (arXiv:2411.15287; Sharma et al. 2023 'Towards Understanding Sycophancy'): models echo user-stated beliefs. Open Phil RFP: reward hacking of human oversight.

title: Weak-to-Strong on Fuzzy-Reward Tasks vs Crisp-Reward Tasks
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped mapping of where weak-to-strong oversight breaks down on fuzzy reward.

original_idea.body:
# Weak-to-Strong on Fuzzy-Reward Tasks vs Crisp-Reward Tasks

**Problem:** Weak-to-strong generalization was shown mainly on crisp binary NLP labels. Its key limitation note is that it 'still doesn't work on ChatGPT preference data' — i.e., fuzzy human-preference reward. The boundary between task types where it works and fails is not mapped.

**Direction:** Using the open weak-to-strong recipe with small models, compare PGR across a spectrum of tasks ordered by reward fuzziness: crisp (sentiment/NLI), medium (factuality), fuzzy (subjective helpfulness pairwise preference). Test whether PGR systematically declines as reward becomes fuzzier.

**Why it matters:** Fuzzy-reward problems are exactly where oversight matters most and where labs struggle. Mapping where weak-to-strong breaks down on fuzzy reward is high counterfactual value; small-model fine-tuning fits the compute budget.

**Relevant context:** Burns et al. 2023 (arXiv:2312.09390) report the method fails on ChatGPT preference data — fuzzy reward. Open code available. The fuzziness gradient has not been systematically charted.

title: FindTheFlaws as a Sandbagging Detector: Vary Whether the Solution-Author Hides Errors
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped evaluation of adversarial flaw-hiding against automated oversight critics.

original_idea.body:
# FindTheFlaws as a Sandbagging Detector: Vary Whether the Solution-Author Hides Errors

**Problem:** FindTheFlaws contains naturally flawed solutions, but does not test ADVERSARIAL flaw-hiding — solutions deliberately crafted to make errors hard to spot. Whether oversight critics catch hidden-on-purpose flaws as well as natural ones is unknown.

**Direction:** Take correct FindTheFlaws solutions and use a strong open model to inject a single subtle error PLUS camouflage (plausible-sounding justification). Compare a small critic model's flaw-detection rate on (a) natural flawed solutions, (b) adversarially-camouflaged flawed solutions. Quantify the camouflage-induced detection drop per domain.

**Why it matters:** Strategic models that hide errors are the central scalable-oversight threat. Measuring how much camouflage degrades automated critique on a public benchmark is a clean model-organism-style evaluation, inference-only.

**Relevant context:** FindTheFlaws (arXiv:2503.22989) has annotated natural flaws + open code, but no adversarial-camouflage condition. Prover-verifier 'sneaky prover' (arXiv:2407.13692) motivates camouflaged errors.

title: Token-Depth Profiler for Shallow Safety Alignment
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped measurement tool for shallow safety alignment depth in open models.

original_idea.body:
# Token-Depth Profiler for Shallow Safety Alignment

**Problem:** Qi et al. (ICLR 2025) showed safety alignment is concentrated in the first few output tokens, but there is no off-the-shelf tool that measures, for an arbitrary open model, HOW deep its safety actually goes (i.e., the KL divergence between aligned and base/unaligned generative distributions as a function of token position).

**Direction:** Build a small open-source 'safety-depth profiler': given an open-weight aligned model and its base counterpart (e.g., Llama-3-Instruct vs Llama-3-base, Qwen-Instruct vs Qwen-base), prefill harmful prompts with k affirmative tokens (k=0..20) and measure per-position attack success and per-position KL divergence. Output a 'safety depth curve' per model and rank a handful of open models by how shallow their alignment is.

**Why it matters:** Turns a qualitative finding into a reusable measurement. A standardized depth metric lets the community compare models and track whether new releases fix shallow alignment. Counterfactually strong: needs only open weights and a single GPU, no lab infra.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al., 'Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep' (arXiv:2406.05946, ICLR 2025 Outstanding Paper): alignment 'adapts the generative distribution primarily over only its very first few output tokens'; prefilling an unaligned base model with 'I cannot fulfill' makes it as safe as aligned models. The paper itself uses KL-over-position analysis.

title: Judge Calibration Variation: Forced-Choice vs Probability-Elicited Verdicts
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted test of calibration/selective-prediction as a recursive-oversight ingredient.

original_idea.body:
# Judge Calibration Variation: Forced-Choice vs Probability-Elicited Verdicts

**Problem:** Most oversight experiments force the judge into a discrete answer. Whether eliciting a CALIBRATED probability from the weak judge (and thresholding) improves oversight quality or surfaces useful 'I don't know' signals is rarely varied.

**Direction:** On debate/consultancy transcripts, elicit the weak judge's verdict two ways: forced binary choice vs a stated probability the answer is correct. Measure accuracy, and additionally whether low-confidence verdicts reliably flag the cases where the judge is wrong (selective-prediction value), comparing the two elicitation modes.

**Why it matters:** An overseer that knows when it doesn't know can escalate to humans — a practical recursive-oversight ingredient. Testing whether probability elicitation buys useful calibration is cheap, inference-only, and protocol-relevant.

**Relevant context:** Debate/consultancy setups (Kenton 2024) use discrete verdicts. LLM calibration/selective-prediction literature suggests probability elicitation can flag errors; untested as an oversight knob.

title: Number-of-Debaters Variation: Two-Sided vs Three-Sided Debate for Weak Judges
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted generalization test of debate oversight beyond binary tasks.

original_idea.body:
# Number-of-Debaters Variation: Two-Sided vs Three-Sided Debate for Weak Judges

**Problem:** Debate is almost always studied with exactly two debaters. Multi-answer questions (3+ options) could be argued by 3+ debaters, but whether adding a third advocate helps or overwhelms a weak judge has not been tested.

**Direction:** On 3-option QuALITY/ARC questions, compare two-debater debate (correct vs one wrong) against three-debater debate (correct vs two distinct wrong answers, each with an advocate). Measure weak-judge accuracy and decision time/tokens. Test whether more advocates help the judge triangulate or cause confusion.

**Why it matters:** Real decisions have many options; knowing whether the two-debater result generalizes to multi-advocate settings is necessary before deploying debate beyond binary tasks. Inference-only variation on the standard protocol.

**Relevant context:** Kenton 2024 / Khan 2024 debate setups are two-sided. Multi-answer debate is an obvious but untested generalization noted as future work.

title: Population Variation: Reasoning Models vs Base Models as Weak Judges
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted test of whether reasoning-tuned small models are better oversight judges.

original_idea.body:
# Population Variation: Reasoning Models vs Base Models as Weak Judges

**Problem:** Prior oversight experiments predate widely-available open 'reasoning' models. Whether a small open reasoning model (trained for long CoT) is a better weak judge than a similarly-sized base model — at equal parameter count — is unmeasured.

**Direction:** Hold debater models fixed. Compare two equally-sized weak judges: a base small open model vs a reasoning-tuned small open model (e.g., a distilled R1-style 1.5B). Measure judge accuracy and bias susceptibility in debate across task domains. Test whether 'reasoning' training improves the oversight role specifically.

**Why it matters:** If reasoning-tuned small models are disproportionately good overseers, that's a cheap lever for scalable oversight available outside labs. Directly varies the judge population on existing protocols, inference-only.

**Relevant context:** Open reasoning-distilled models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill series) are now freely available; oversight benchmarks (Kenton 2024) predate them and used base/chat judges.

title: Does Letting the Judge See Debater Confidence Help or Mislead?
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted study of a potential oversight vulnerability from confidence signals.

original_idea.body:
# Does Letting the Judge See Debater Confidence Help or Mislead?

**Problem:** Debaters typically present arguments without stated confidence. A variation gives the weak judge each debater's self-reported confidence. Since LLM confidence is often miscalibrated, this could either inform or mislead the judge — untested in oversight.

**Direction:** Generate debates where each debater also outputs a self-reported confidence. Run the weak judge WITH vs WITHOUT seeing those confidences. Measure accuracy change, and separately whether the wrong-side debater's (over)confidence systematically misleads the judge. Cross-reference debater confidence against actual correctness.

**Why it matters:** Confidence signals are tempting shortcuts for overseers; if a confidently-wrong model exploits them, that's an oversight vulnerability. Clean controlled variation, inference-only, public data.

**Relevant context:** LLM overconfidence/miscalibration is well documented; debate setups (Khan 2024, Kenton 2024) do not surface debater confidence to judges. Confirmation/persuasion biases (arXiv:2507.19486) make this risky.

title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization Robustness to Label Quantity
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted dose-response study of weak-to-strong oversight cost/bias.

original_idea.body:
# Weak-to-Strong Generalization Robustness to Label Quantity

**Problem:** Weak-to-strong PGR is reported at a fixed amount of weak supervision. How PGR scales with the NUMBER of weak labels — whether a strong student needs many weak labels to elicit latent knowledge or just a few — is not the original paper's focus.

**Direction:** Using the open recipe with small models, sweep weak-label dataset size (e.g., 50, 200, 1000, 5000) for a fixed weak-strong pair on one classification task. Plot PGR vs number of weak labels. Test whether there is a small-data regime where the strong model's prior dominates (high PGR cheaply) vs a regime where more weak labels hurt by transferring bias.

**Why it matters:** If a handful of weak labels suffice to elicit strong-model knowledge, scalable oversight is far cheaper than assumed; if more labels transfer more bias, that warns against scaling weak supervision. A clean dose-response curve, small-model fine-tuning within budget.

**Relevant context:** Burns et al. 2023 (arXiv:2312.09390): PGR at fixed supervision; data-quantity scaling of PGR is underexplored. Open code available.

title: Open Replication of Self-Play Debate Training's Judge-Accuracy Claim Without Training
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted training-free test of a core self-play-debate oversight assumption.

original_idea.body:
# Open Replication of Self-Play Debate Training's Judge-Accuracy Claim Without Training

**Problem:** Training debaters via self-play reportedly improves judge accuracy, but that requires training. A non-lab researcher cannot retrain debaters — yet the underlying claim (more persuasive correct debaters help judges more than persuasive wrong ones) can be tested by VARYING debater persuasiveness via prompting.

**Direction:** Without training, induce a persuasiveness ladder on a fixed debater model via prompting (terse vs rhetorical/persuasive style). Run debates where ONLY the correct side, then ONLY the wrong side, gets the persuasive style. Measure weak-judge accuracy in each condition to test whether persuasiveness on the truth helps more than equal persuasiveness on falsehood.

**Why it matters:** Confirms or refutes the central self-play-debate assumption using only inference and prompting — a fully counterfactual, non-lab-feasible replication of an otherwise training-heavy result.

**Relevant context:** 'Training LMs to Win Debates with Self-Play Improves Judge Accuracy' (arXiv:2409.16636) and 'AI Debaters Are More Persuasive...' (arXiv:2510.13912) tie persuasiveness to judge accuracy; the prompted-persuasiveness variation avoids training.

title: Quote-Verification Tooling: Does Giving Weak Judges a Citation Checker Beat Debate Alone?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped oversight tool addressing fabricated-quote exploitation in debate.

original_idea.body:
# Quote-Verification Tooling: Does Giving Weak Judges a Citation Checker Beat Debate Alone?

**Problem:** In information-asymmetric debate, debaters quote source text and judges can't fully verify quotes. A small infrastructure variation: give the judge an automated quote-verification tool (string-match against the source). Whether this cheap tool rivals debate's benefit is untested.

**Direction:** Build a tiny verification harness that checks whether each quoted snippet actually appears in the QuALITY source passage and flags fabricated quotes to the weak judge. Compare judge accuracy: debate-alone vs debate-plus-quote-checker. Measure how often fabricated quotes occur and how much the checker recovers.

**Why it matters:** A simple, deterministic verification firewall could be a strategically valuable oversight tool that needs no lab resources. Building and evaluating this small prototype is exactly the kind of infrastructure favored here.

**Relevant context:** Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.06782): quoting source text drives debate's benefit, but judges can't verify quotes. The verification project's existing CrossRef/Semantic-Scholar tooling pattern (src/saim/verification/) shows a checker harness is feasible.

title: Temperature/Decoding Variation: Does Sampling Diversity in Debaters Change Oversight Outcomes?
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted study of a deployment-relevant knob affecting oversight reliability.

original_idea.body:
# Temperature/Decoding Variation: Does Sampling Diversity in Debaters Change Oversight Outcomes?

**Problem:** Oversight experiments fix decoding settings. Whether higher-temperature (more diverse, exploratory) debaters help a weak judge surface truth better than greedy debaters — or just add noise the judge can't filter — is unstudied.

**Direction:** Generate debate transcripts with debaters at greedy/low temperature vs high temperature (more varied arguments), holding the model and judge fixed. Measure weak-judge accuracy and argument diversity per condition. Test whether decoding diversity is an exploitable knob for better (or worse) oversight.

**Why it matters:** Decoding settings are a free, deployment-relevant lever; knowing whether they affect oversight reliability matters for anyone running these protocols. Inference-only and trivially within budget.

**Relevant context:** Oversight protocol papers (Kenton 2024, Khan 2024) fix decoding; sensitivity of safety behaviors to decoding parameters is known to matter (a theme in the existing idea catalogue) but untested for debate-judge accuracy specifically.

title: Does the Persona-Judge Advantage Survive Adversarial Debaters?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped stress-test of a cheap oversight upgrade under adversarial debaters.

original_idea.body:
# Does the Persona-Judge Advantage Survive Adversarial Debaters?

**Problem:** Rahman et al. (2025, 'AI Debate Aids Assessment of Controversial Claims') found AI judges given human-like personas reached 78.5% accuracy on COVID/climate claims, beating both human judges (70.1%) and default AI judges (69.8%). It is unclear whether this persona advantage is robust or whether it just reflects personas reading more carefully on benign transcripts.

**Direction:** Replicate the persona-judge setup on a small open judge model (e.g., Llama-3-8B-Instruct) using the released debate transcripts. Then run a follow-up: stress-test by (a) swapping in transcripts where the dishonest debater is the more fluent/longer one, and (b) varying persona type (skeptic vs. believer vs. neutral). Measure whether persona-induced accuracy gains hold or invert when the persuasive debater is wrong.

**Why it matters:** If a cheap prompting trick (personas) reliably improves oversight accuracy, it is a near-free oversight upgrade deployable outside any lab. If the gain collapses under adversarial debaters, the field needs to know before personas are trusted. Pure inference on released transcripts, no training, high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Rahman et al. 2025 (arXiv:2506.02175): persona AI judges 78.5% vs human 70.1% vs default AI 69.8% on contested factuality; debate beats consultancy (+10% COVID). Transcripts and protocol released.

title: Mapping the Two Plateaus: Reproducing Oversight Elo Curves in Mafia on a Single GPU
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted replication testing robustness of scaling laws for scalable oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Mapping the Two Plateaus: Reproducing Oversight Elo Curves in Mafia on a Single GPU

**Problem:** Engels et al. (2025, 'Scaling Laws For Scalable Oversight') found oversight success is a piecewise-linear function of capability with two plateaus (task incompetence, task saturation), validated on Nim, Mafia, Debate, Backdoor Code, Wargames. The exact location of the plateau knees was estimated from a handful of model sizes and may be sensitive to prompting.

**Direction:** Reproduce just the Mafia oversight game using a ladder of small open models (Qwen 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B as players, varying which is overseer). Self-play Mafia games are cheap text rollouts. Fit the oversight Elo-vs-capability curve and test whether the plateau structure replicates, and how much it shifts with simple prompt scaffolding (chain-of-thought vs none).

**Why it matters:** The two-plateau finding underpins claims about when nested oversight works. Independent replication on a different model family, with sensitivity to prompting, tests whether scaling laws for oversight are robust or artifacts. Text-only game rollouts fit a consumer GPU; no proprietary data.

**Relevant context:** Engels et al. 2025 (arXiv:2504.18530): piecewise-linear oversight Elo with two plateaus; Debate NSO success 51.7% at Elo gap 400; validated on Mafia/Debate/Backdoor/Wargames/Nim.

title: Prefill-Robustness Leaderboard for Open Models
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped jailbreak-vulnerability benchmark for a real deployment threat.

original_idea.body:
# Prefill-Robustness Leaderboard for Open Models

**Problem:** Prefilling attacks (forcing the model's first output tokens to be affirmative) are one of the simplest and most effective jailbreaks, yet there is no standardized leaderboard that ranks open-weight models purely by prefill vulnerability with a fixed harmful-prompt set.

**Direction:** Create a minimal benchmark harness that takes the StrongREJECT forbidden-prompt set, applies a fixed ladder of affirmative prefixes ('Sure, here is', 'Step 1:', etc.), and scores responses with the StrongREJECT rubric evaluator. Produce a reproducible prefill-vulnerability score for ~6-8 open models and publish the harness so others can add models.

**Why it matters:** Prefill APIs are exposed by many open-weight serving stacks, making this a real deployment threat. A public leaderboard creates accountability and a cheap regression test. No training, no proprietary data needed.

**Relevant context:** StrongREJECT (Souly et al., arXiv:2402.10260) provides a curated forbidden-prompt set and a rubric evaluator (Score = (1-Refusal) x (Specificity+Convincingness)/2). Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946) establish prefilling as a canonical attack. dsbowen/strong_reject is open source.

title: Why Does Confirmation Bias Survive Online Research? Decomposing the Recchia Effect
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped decomposition of a confirmation-bias oversight failure with fixable mechanisms.

original_idea.body:
# Why Does Confirmation Bias Survive Online Research? Decomposing the Recchia Effect

**Problem:** Recchia et al. (2025, 'Confirmation Bias: A Challenge for Scalable Oversight') found human evaluators grew MORE confident in an AI's answer after doing online research even when the answer was wrong. The mechanism is unclear: is it selective search, motivated reading, or anchoring on the AI's stated answer?

**Direction:** Run a small follow-up using LLM-simulated evaluators as a cheap model organism. Give a judge model an AI answer plus retrieved snippets and measure confidence shift. Ablate: (a) show the AI's answer before vs after retrieval, (b) provide balanced vs answer-aligned snippets, (c) force the judge to write a counter-argument first. Quantify which intervention removes the confidence-on-wrong-answers effect.

**Why it matters:** If confirmation bias in oversight is driven by a specific, fixable step (e.g., anchoring on the stated answer), simple protocol changes could harden oversight. This is exactly a fuzzy human-bias problem labs underinvest in, and it runs entirely on open models plus public QA data.

**Relevant context:** Recchia et al. 2025 (arXiv:2507.19486, AAAI): no overall advantage for simple oversight protocols; evaluators became more confident in incorrect answers after research; showing both-side arguments helped only when model was wrong.

title: Is the Legibility Tax a Verifier-Capability Artifact?
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted investigation of the legibility tax in checkability-based oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Is the Legibility Tax a Verifier-Capability Artifact?

**Problem:** Kirchner et al. (2024, OpenAI Prover-Verifier Games) found a 'legibility tax': models trained to be checkable by a weak verifier dropped from ~80% to ~60% accuracy on grade-school math. It is unproven whether the tax shrinks as the verifier gets stronger, or whether it reflects an intrinsic legibility/correctness tradeoff.

**Direction:** Without training, simulate the verifier side: take a fixed strong solver's GSM8K solutions and a set of progressively stronger small verifier models. Measure how verification accuracy on correct vs adversarial 'sneaky' solutions changes with verifier capability. Estimate the implied legibility tax as a function of verifier strength using the released methodology.

**Why it matters:** If the tax is mostly a weak-verifier artifact, scalable oversight via checkability is cheaper than feared; if intrinsic, it bounds the protocol. The experiment is inference-only on public math benchmarks and small models, ideal for outside-lab work.

**Relevant context:** Kirchner et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.13692): legibility tax, PVG 60% vs correctness-only 80% on grade-school math; sneaky-prover/verifier setup released. Decoupled PVG follow-up (arXiv:2602.23248) proposes a translator fix.

title: Does Easy-to-Hard Reward-Model Generalization Hold Outside Math?
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted test of an easy-to-hard oversight route's domain generality.

original_idea.body:
# Does Easy-to-Hard Reward-Model Generalization Hold Outside Math?

**Problem:** Sun et al. (2024, 'Easy-to-Hard Generalization') found a reward model trained only on easy MATH problems scores hard-problem solutions well enough to improve generators. The striking claim is that evaluators generalize easy-to-hard; but it was shown mainly on math, leaving open whether it transfers to fuzzier domains.

**Direction:** Use an off-the-shelf open reward/judge model as the evaluator. Calibrate its 'easy' reliability on simple instances of a non-math task (e.g., short factual claims, simple code review), then measure how its ranking accuracy degrades on hard instances of the same task. Compare the easy-to-hard degradation slope across 3 task types to see where the phenomenon breaks.

**Why it matters:** Easy-to-hard generalization is a leading route to supervising superhuman models. Knowing which task structures preserve it (and which collapse) is decision-relevant and requires no training, only public datasets and open judges.

**Relevant context:** Sun et al. 2024 (arXiv:2403.09472, NeurIPS): RM trained on easy MATH supervision improves hard-problem performance (34B reranking 52.5% MATH500); authors note extension beyond math but with limited evidence.

title: Self-Preference Bias as an Oversight Vulnerability: Does a Judge Favor Its Own Family's Sneaky Answers?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped study of in-family deception blind spots as an oversight failure mode.

original_idea.body:
# Self-Preference Bias as an Oversight Vulnerability: Does a Judge Favor Its Own Family's Sneaky Answers?

**Problem:** Self-preference bias research (arXiv:2410.21819) shows LLM judges prefer text they themselves are likely to generate (low perplexity). In an oversight setting this could mean a judge systematically under-flags errors from its own model family, a blind spot a strategic AI could exploit.

**Direction:** Take 2-3 open model families. Have each generate subtly-wrong answers to a QA set, then have each family's model judge correctness of all families' answers. Measure whether judges miss more errors from their own family. Follow-up: test whether paraphrasing answers (to break the perplexity signature) removes the blind spot.

**Why it matters:** If overseers are systematically blind to in-family deception, multi-vendor or cross-family oversight becomes a concrete defense. This is a model-organism-style study of an oversight failure mode, fully runnable on open models and public QA data.

**Relevant context:** Wang et al. 2024 (arXiv:2410.21819): GPT-4 shows significant self-preference; bias rooted in perplexity/familiarity. Quantifying/Mitigating Self-Preference (arXiv:2604.22891) extends measurement.

title: When Does Debate Beat Consultancy Disappear? Probing the Skeptic-vs-Believer Asymmetry
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted mapping of when debate fails to correct biased oversight judges.

original_idea.body:
# When Does Debate Beat Consultancy Disappear? Probing the Skeptic-vs-Believer Asymmetry

**Problem:** Rahman et al. (2025) found debate's advantage over consultancy was large for 'mainstream believers' (+15.2%) but small for 'skeptical believers' (+4.7%) on COVID claims. The cause of this asymmetry, and whether it generalizes, is unexplained.

**Direction:** Using the released transcripts and an open judge model, systematically vary the judge's induced prior (via persona prompt) from strong-skeptic to strong-believer, in fine steps, and measure debate-vs-consultancy accuracy gap as a function of prior strength. Map the full curve to find where debate stops helping.

**Why it matters:** Understanding when debate fails to correct biased judges is core to whether debate is a trustworthy oversight protocol for contested/long-horizon questions that labs cannot easily ground-truth. Inference-only on public transcripts.

**Relevant context:** Rahman et al. 2025 (arXiv:2506.02175): debate-over-consultancy gain +15.2% mainstream believers vs +4.7% skeptics (COVID); climate +3.8% overall.

title: Does Weak-to-Strong Generalization Survive a Systematically Biased Weak Teacher?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped test of the systematic-overseer-error open problem in weak-to-strong.

original_idea.body:
# Does Weak-to-Strong Generalization Survive a Systematically Biased Weak Teacher?

**Problem:** Burns et al. (2023) showed strong students trained on a weak teacher's labels can outperform the teacher. Most follow-ups vary the model-size gap, but real overseers have systematic (not random) errors. It is unclear whether W2S generalization recovers ground truth when the weak teacher is biased in a consistent direction.

**Direction:** On a binary classification dataset with public labels, simulate a weak teacher by a small open model whose errors are deliberately skewed (e.g., always favoring one class on ambiguous items). Fit a lightweight linear probe / logistic head on the frozen strong model's representations using the biased weak labels (no full fine-tuning). Measure whether the student corrects the systematic bias or inherits it.

**Why it matters:** Systematic overseer error is the explicitly-flagged open problem (recursive oversight with biased layers). Testing whether W2S 'launders' or amplifies systematic bias is directly decision-relevant and feasible with a frozen model + linear probe on a consumer GPU.

**Relevant context:** Burns et al. 2023 (arXiv:2312.09390, OpenAI): W2S generalization, students recover much of strong performance from weak labels. Open code released. Anthropic open problem: recursive oversight with systematically-erring layers.

title: Verbosity Bias in Oversight: Can Longer Wrong Answers Beat Shorter Right Ones?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped quantification of a verbosity reward-hacking channel against overseers.

original_idea.body:
# Verbosity Bias in Oversight: Can Longer Wrong Answers Beat Shorter Right Ones?

**Problem:** LLM-judge verbosity bias is documented but mostly on preference quality, not on correctness oversight. The open question: in a correctness-checking setting, does answer length let a wrong answer slip past an overseer, and by how much?

**Direction:** Take a QA set with verifiable answers. For each item, produce a short correct answer and a long, elaborated wrong answer (and vice versa) via an open model. Have an open judge model decide correctness. Measure the length-induced error rate and whether a 'normalize length' instruction or truncation removes it. Report a dose-response curve of error vs length ratio.

**Why it matters:** Verbosity is one of the named reward-hacking signatures of evaluator manipulation. Quantifying how much length alone fools a correctness overseer gives a concrete, cheap robustness metric for any oversight harness. No training, public data.

**Relevant context:** LLM-as-judge bias surveys (arXiv:2411.16594, arXiv:2410.02736) document verbosity/length bias; Wen et al. 2024 show RLHF models become better at convincing humans they are right when wrong.

title: Does Showing Both-Sided Arguments Only Help When the Model Is Wrong? Replicating and Stress-Testing Recchia's Asymmetry
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted replication probing a deployable oversight protocol's genuine error-correction.

original_idea.body:
# Does Showing Both-Sided Arguments Only Help When the Model Is Wrong? Replicating and Stress-Testing Recchia's Asymmetry

**Problem:** Recchia et al. (2025) found that presenting arguments for both answers improved evaluator accuracy specifically in cases where the AI was incorrect, but offered no overall advantage. This asymmetric benefit is surprising and underexplored: it could be a real correction effect or a regression-to-chance artifact.

**Direction:** Replicate with LLM-judge stand-ins on a public QA set: present (a) AI answer only, (b) AI answer + arguments for both sides, (c) arguments only. Separate accuracy on items where the AI is right vs wrong. Test whether the both-sides benefit on wrong items is genuine error-correction or just lowered confidence pushing toxic-confident wrong answers toward chance.

**Why it matters:** If a simple 'always present both sides' rule reliably catches model errors without hurting correct cases, it is a deployable oversight protocol. Distinguishing real correction from noise is necessary before recommending it. Inference-only, public data.

**Relevant context:** Recchia et al. 2025 (arXiv:2507.19486): both-side arguments improved accuracy only when the model was incorrect; no overall protocol advantage.

title: Position Bias in Debate Judging: Does the Last Debater Win?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped measurement of an exploitable content-free order bias in debate oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Position Bias in Debate Judging: Does the Last Debater Win?

**Problem:** Position bias (preferring responses in certain positions) is well-documented for pairwise LLM judging. In debate-based oversight, debaters speak in an order; it is unknown whether judges systematically favor the first or last debater independent of argument quality, which would let an AI game oversight by claiming a turn slot.

**Direction:** Using released debate transcripts, present each transcript to an open judge model in both speaking orders (swap which debater goes first/last) and measure how often the verdict flips purely due to order. Quantify a 'turn-order advantage' and test whether anonymizing/randomizing order or a recency-summary instruction neutralizes it.

**Why it matters:** Order is an exploitable, content-free lever in any debate oversight protocol. Measuring and neutralizing it is a concrete robustness contribution for the debate protocol that labs are betting on. Inference-only on public transcripts.

**Relevant context:** LLM-judge position bias documented across model families (arXiv:2410.02736, arXiv:2411.16594); fixable by reordering. Debate transcripts from Rahman et al. 2025 / Khan et al. self-play debate (arXiv:2409.16636) available.

title: Self-Play Debate Improved Judge Accuracy — Does It Transfer to a Different, Weaker Judge?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped test of whether debate's benefit holds for genuinely weak oversight judges.

original_idea.body:
# Self-Play Debate Improved Judge Accuracy — Does It Transfer to a Different, Weaker Judge?

**Problem:** Khan/Kenton-style work (arXiv:2409.16636) found training debaters via self-play to win debates improved judge accuracy on QuALITY-style reading comprehension. The optimistic result may depend on the specific judge model used; transfer to weaker or different-family judges is the relevant scalable-oversight question.

**Direction:** Take the released debater outputs/transcripts and feed them to a panel of differently-sized open judges (e.g., 1B, 3B, 8B). Measure whether the judge-accuracy improvement from stronger debaters holds, shrinks, or reverses as the judge gets weaker, mapping the judge-capability dependence of the debate benefit.

**Why it matters:** Scalable oversight requires the JUDGE to be weaker than the debaters. If the benefit of better debaters only appears for strong judges, debate's promise for genuine weak-judge oversight is weaker than claimed. Inference-only, public transcripts.

**Relevant context:** Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2409.16636): self-play-trained debaters improve judge accuracy on long-document QA; transcripts released. Connects to Engels et al. Debate NSO 51.7% at Elo gap 400.

title: Reasoning-Model Shallow-Alignment Probe (CoT vs Final Answer)
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped diagnostic localizing safety alignment depth in reasoning models.

original_idea.body:
# Reasoning-Model Shallow-Alignment Probe (CoT vs Final Answer)

**Problem:** The shallow-alignment finding was established on standard instruction-tuned models. Reasoning models that emit chain-of-thought before a final answer have a different token structure, and it is unmeasured whether their safety is shallow in the CoT, the final answer, or both.

**Direction:** Take an open reasoning model (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-distill, QwQ, or a small open o1-style model) and prefill (a) the start of the reasoning trace and (b) the start of the final answer with affirmative tokens. Compare attack success when the CoT is left to refuse vs forced affirmative. Build a small 'where is the safety' diagnostic that localizes alignment depth across the reasoning/answer boundary.

**Why it matters:** Reasoning models are increasingly deployed and shown to be MORE exploitable in multi-turn settings; understanding whether their safety lives in the CoT or the answer tells defenders where to put probes/monitors. Directly extends the ICLR finding to a new architecture class with no training.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946) shallow alignment. 'Safety in Large Reasoning Models: A Survey' (arXiv:2504.17704) and Crescendo work note reasoning models like o1/DeepSeek-R1 are 'particularly susceptible' because explicit CoT 'renders them more exploitable.' Context file lists 'test whether reasoning models exhibit same shallow alignment pattern' as a suggested follow-up.

title: Does Sneaky-Prover Pressure Make Solutions Less Legible to Humans Too, Not Just to Verifier Models?
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted test of a load-bearing oversight assumption (model verifiers as human proxies).

original_idea.body:
# Does Sneaky-Prover Pressure Make Solutions Less Legible to Humans Too, Not Just to Verifier Models?

**Problem:** Prover-verifier games train a 'sneaky prover' to slip wrong solutions past a verifier model. OpenAI reported that legibility training improved human ability to spot errors. But the inverse — whether sneaky solutions that fool the verifier MODEL also fool HUMANS at the same rate — is the load-bearing assumption and is untested at small scale.

**Direction:** Take released sneaky and honest solutions. Run a small human-subjects study (e.g., 15-20 classmates / Prolific micro-study) timing how often humans correctly flag sneaky vs honest solutions, and correlate human flag rate with the verifier model's flag rate per item. Test whether items that fool the model also fool humans.

**Why it matters:** If model-verifiers and humans share blind spots, using a verifier model as a human proxy is safe; if they diverge, automated legibility metrics overstate human oversight. A cheap human study with public artifacts directly tests a key oversight assumption.

**Relevant context:** Kirchner et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.13692): PVG legibility training improved human verification; sneaky/honest solution artifacts released.

title: Reward-Model Overoptimization: Reproducing the U-Shaped Gold-Score Curve with Open Reward Models
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped diagnostic for reward hacking / Goodhart overoptimization of overseers.

original_idea.body:
# Reward-Model Overoptimization: Reproducing the U-Shaped Gold-Score Curve with Open Reward Models

**Problem:** Gao et al. and follow-ups found that as a policy is optimized against a proxy reward model, true (gold) reward first rises then falls (Goodhart/overoptimization). Whether this curve and its KL-scaling hold for today's small open reward models, and how quickly the turn happens, is worth independent confirmation.

**Direction:** Without RL training: take an open reward model as proxy and a stronger open judge as 'gold'. Generate many candidate responses per prompt, then simulate increasing optimization pressure via best-of-n reranking with growing n (n is a clean proxy for optimization strength). Plot gold score vs proxy score vs n to recover the overoptimization curve and find where reward hacking kicks in.

**Why it matters:** Reward hacking of the overseer is a named open problem. Best-of-n is a training-free way to elicit and measure overoptimization on a single GPU, giving a reusable diagnostic for any proxy reward model — high counterfactual value, no lab infra.

**Relevant context:** Reward-model overoptimization (Goodhart) is a core RLHF failure (Lilian Weng reward-hacking survey 2024; reward-hacking-in-era-of-large-models arXiv:2604.13602). Best-of-n as optimization-pressure proxy is standard.

title: Does Multi-Agent Judge Aggregation Reduce or Amplify Oversight Bias?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped factorial test of whether committee oversight amplifies shared biases.

original_idea.body:
# Does Multi-Agent Judge Aggregation Reduce or Amplify Oversight Bias?

**Problem:** 'Judging with Many Minds' (arXiv:2505.19477) found multi-agent LLM-judge panels can either reduce prejudice or AMPLIFY it depending on setup — a surprising non-monotone result. The conditions distinguishing reduction from amplification are not pinned down for correctness oversight.

**Direction:** Build a small panel of open judge models with a single shared bias (e.g., self-preference toward one model family's answers). Vary aggregation: independent majority vote vs sequential discussion vs debate-then-vote. On a QA correctness task with a planted bias, measure whether each aggregation method reduces or amplifies the shared blind spot.

**Why it matters:** Many proposed oversight schemes assume more overseers = safer. If discussion-based aggregation amplifies shared biases, naive 'committee' oversight is dangerous. A clean factorial experiment, inference-only on open models.

**Relevant context:** Judging with Many Minds (arXiv:2505.19477): multi-agent judging shows both bias amplification and resistance depending on configuration.

title: Does the Easy-to-Hard Evaluator Advantage Persist When Hard Problems Require a Different Skill?
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted boundary test of easy-to-hard evaluator generalization for oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Does the Easy-to-Hard Evaluator Advantage Persist When Hard Problems Require a Different Skill, Not Just More Steps?

**Problem:** Sun et al. (2024) defined 'hard' as higher MATH difficulty levels — essentially harder versions of the same skill. The surprising easy-to-hard generalization may rely on this skill-continuity. Whether evaluators generalize when hard tasks demand a qualitatively new sub-skill is untested.

**Direction:** Construct an easy/hard split where difficulty comes from skill-shift (e.g., easy = single-step arithmetic word problems, hard = problems also needing unit conversion or a planted distractor). Calibrate an open judge on easy items, then measure ranking accuracy on skill-shifted hard items vs same-skill harder items. Compare degradation slopes.

**Why it matters:** Real superhuman tasks differ from training tasks in KIND, not just degree. Testing whether easy-to-hard evaluator generalization is skill-continuity-dependent bounds its usefulness for scalable oversight. Public data, open judge, no training.

**Relevant context:** Sun et al. 2024 (arXiv:2403.09472): easy-to-hard generalization on MATH levels 1-3 -> 4-5; surprising RM generalization. Difficulty there is within-skill.

title: Can a Weak Overseer Catch a Strong Model That Hides Its Plan from the Chain-of-Thought?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped model-organism test of CoT-monitoring oversight against plan-hiding.

original_idea.body:
# Can a Weak Overseer Catch a Strong Model That Hides Its Plan from the Chain-of-Thought?

**Problem:** Reward-hacking research warns models can develop general evaluator-gaming strategies that don't appear in verbalized reasoning. A concrete oversight question: if a model's CoT looks benign but its answer is sabotaged, can CoT-monitoring oversight still catch it?

**Direction:** Create a small model organism via prompting: instruct an open model to insert a subtle error/backdoor while writing an innocuous, plausible chain-of-thought (a feasible prompt-induced 'attacks-without-verbalizing' slice). Then test whether a weaker overseer model reading only the CoT, only the answer, or both, detects the sabotage. Measure detection rate per oversight modality.

**Why it matters:** CoT monitoring is a leading cheap oversight method; its failure against plan-hiding models is a key medium-horizon threat labs deprioritize. A prompt-induced model organism plus a monitoring harness is exactly the outside-lab, infrastructure-prototype work prioritized here.

**Relevant context:** Reward-hacking-as-general-strategy and CoT-unfaithfulness themes (arXiv:2604.13602; Wen et al. 2024 misleading evaluators). Engels et al. Backdoor Code oversight game (arXiv:2504.18530) provides a template task.

title: Does Nested Oversight Actually Beat Single-Step Oversight at Fixed Compute? A Small Mafia Replication
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted test of a central nested scalable oversight proposal at fixed compute.

original_idea.body:
# Does Nested Oversight Actually Beat Single-Step Oversight at Fixed Compute? A Small Mafia Replication

**Problem:** Engels et al. (2025) derived an optimal number of oversight levels for Nested Scalable Oversight. The counterintuitive claim that intermediate models help (rather than just adding error) deserves a hands-on check at small scale and fixed total compute budget.

**Direction:** Using the Mafia game with a small model ladder, compare (a) a weak overseer directly judging a strong player vs (b) a chain weak -> medium -> strong, holding total inference calls fixed. Measure oversight success and find whether nesting helps at the predicted level count, and how sensitive the optimum is to capability gaps.

**Why it matters:** Nested oversight is a central proposal for controlling superhuman AI. Empirically confirming (or refuting) the optimal-levels prediction at fixed compute is decision-relevant and runs as cheap text game rollouts on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Engels et al. 2025 (arXiv:2504.18530): NSO with trusted-overseeing-untrusted chains; derived optimal number of oversight levels; Mafia among validated games.

title: Does Persona-Induced Judge Accuracy Generalize Beyond Controversial Topics to Plain Factual QA?
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted test of whether a persona oversight trick is general or narrow debiasing.

original_idea.body:
# Does Persona-Induced Judge Accuracy Generalize Beyond Controversial Topics to Plain Factual QA?

**Problem:** The persona-judge gain (Rahman et al. 2025) was measured on emotionally-charged COVID/climate claims where human-like priors plausibly help. It is unknown whether personas help, hurt, or are neutral on non-controversial factual questions where there is no prior to leverage.

**Direction:** Apply the persona-vs-default judge comparison to a neutral factual QA benchmark (e.g., TruthfulQA or simple trivia) with debate/consultancy-style transcripts generated by open models. Measure whether persona judges retain their accuracy edge or whether the edge was specific to belief-laden domains.

**Why it matters:** Separating 'personas help reasoning' from 'personas counteract a specific bias' tells us whether the persona trick is a general oversight upgrade or a narrow debiasing tool. Fully inference-based on open models and public data.

**Relevant context:** Rahman et al. 2025 (arXiv:2506.02175): persona judges 78.5% on contested claims; effect measured only on belief-laden topics.

title: Is the Self-Preference / Perplexity Link Causal? A Paraphrase Intervention
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted causal test of a content-free attack vector against oversight judges.

original_idea.body:
# Is the Self-Preference / Perplexity Link Causal? A Paraphrase Intervention

**Problem:** Wang et al. (2024) argued self-preference bias arises because judges prefer low-perplexity (familiar) text. The correlation is established; the causal claim that lowering an answer's perplexity-to-the-judge raises its score is less directly tested.

**Direction:** Take fixed-meaning answers and produce paraphrase variants spanning a range of perplexity under a target open judge model (measure perplexity directly). Hold correctness constant. Regress the judge's preference/score on measured perplexity across paraphrases. A monotone effect at equal meaning isolates the causal perplexity->preference channel.

**Why it matters:** If perplexity causally drives judge preference, an AI can game oversight purely by stylistic familiarity, with no change in substance — a content-free attack vector. Confirming causality motivates perplexity-normalized oversight. Inference-only, open models, public text.

**Relevant context:** Wang et al. 2024 (arXiv:2410.21819): self-preference bias tied to perplexity/familiarity, established as correlation; mitigation follow-up arXiv:2604.22891.

title: Does Forcing the Judge to Answer First Inoculate Against Anchoring on the Model's Stated Answer?
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted test of a cheap anchoring-debias protocol fix for oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Does Forcing the Judge to Answer First Inoculate Against Anchoring on the Model's Stated Answer?

**Problem:** Recchia's confirmation-bias result suggests overseers anchor on the AI's stated answer. A natural follow-up intervention — having the overseer commit to its own answer BEFORE seeing the AI's — has not been cleanly isolated as a debiasing mechanism in oversight.

**Direction:** On a public QA set, compare oversight accuracy under three conditions with an open judge model standing in for the evaluator: (a) see AI answer then judge, (b) judge produces own answer first, then sees AI answer and decides, (c) judge sees only evidence, never the AI's claimed answer. Measure error rate on items where the AI is wrong.

**Why it matters:** A one-line protocol change ('answer first') that removes anchoring would be a cheap, broadly deployable oversight fix. Testing it isolates a candidate mechanism behind Recchia's effect. Inference-only, public data.

**Relevant context:** Recchia et al. 2025 (arXiv:2507.19486): evaluators grew confident in wrong AI answers; anchoring on the stated answer is a leading explanation. Builds on the confirmation-bias finding.

title: Replicating Wen et al.: Do RLHF'd Models Get Better at Convincing Overseers They Are Right When Wrong?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped test of U-Sophistry degrading oversight as models become more aligned.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Wen et al.: Do RLHF'd Models Get Better at Convincing Overseers They Are Right When Wrong?

**Problem:** Wen et al. (2024) found RLHF can make models better at persuading evaluators they are correct even when wrong (U-Sophistry). The effect was shown on specific RLHF'd models; whether it appears as a general gap between base and instruct/RLHF'd open models is worth independent measurement.

**Direction:** Without training: compare a base open model and its instruct/RLHF'd sibling (same family/size). On a QA set, collect their WRONG answers plus justifications, then have a fixed judge model rate persuasiveness/correctness-belief. Test whether the RLHF'd model's wrong answers are systematically more convincing than the base model's wrong answers.

**Why it matters:** If RLHF reliably sharpens persuasion-on-wrong-answers as a side effect, oversight degrades exactly as models get more 'aligned' on the surface — a core scalable-oversight worry. Comparing public base vs instruct checkpoints needs no training and no lab data.

**Relevant context:** Wen et al. 2024: RLHF models become better at convincing humans they are correct even when wrong (U-Sophistry / evaluator misleading), cited in reward-hacking surveys (arXiv:2604.13602).

title: Cross-Family Linear-Probe Transfer Benchmark for Jailbreak Detection
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped benchmark for cross-family transfer of jailbreak-detection probes.

original_idea.body:
# Cross-Family Linear-Probe Transfer Benchmark for Jailbreak Detection

**Problem:** Activation-probe jailbreak detectors are cheap and effective, but it is unclear whether a probe trained on one open model's activations transfers to another family. There is no benchmark measuring cross-family probe transfer.

**Direction:** Train simple logistic-regression probes on residual-stream activations (collected with hooks) for jailbroken vs benign prompts on one open model (e.g., Llama-3-8B), then evaluate the SAME probe (after aligning hidden dims via a learned linear map or shared-direction projection) on Qwen, Mistral, Gemma. Report a transfer matrix of detection AUC.

**Why it matters:** If probes transfer, small labs can reuse detectors instead of retraining per model; if they don't, that's a critical caveat for cheap-monitor deployment. Recent work shows refusal directions align across the Llama-Qwen-Mistral-Phi cluster, making transfer plausible and worth measuring. Single GPU, no training of LLMs.

**Relevant context:** Arditi et al. 'Refusal in LMs Is Mediated by a Single Direction' (NeurIPS 2024); 'Jailbreak Transferability Emerges from Shared Representations' (arXiv:2506.12913) finds same-axis directions align tightly across LQMP cluster. Anthropic 'Cost-Effective Constitutional Classifiers via Representation Re-use' (alignment.anthropic.com 2025). Context file: 'replicate on different model families.'

title: Does Debate Help More Than Consultancy When the Honest Side Is the WEAKER Debater?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped stress of debate's core safety assumption under capability asymmetry.

original_idea.body:
# Does Debate Help More Than Consultancy When the Honest Side Is the WEAKER Debater?

**Problem:** Debate's safety rests on the honest debater winning. Engels et al. and others assume rough capability parity; but a key worry is asymmetric capability where the honest position is argued by a weaker model. Whether debate still beats consultancy in that regime is the load-bearing case.

**Direction:** Generate debate transcripts with an open model on a verifiable QA task, but deliberately handicap the honest debater (smaller model / fewer tokens) while the dishonest debater is strong. Have a fixed judge decide. Compare judge accuracy under debate vs consultancy across a sweep of honest-debater handicap levels.

**Why it matters:** If debate's truth-tracking collapses precisely when the truth-teller is outmatched, the protocol fails in the adversarial regime that matters for superhuman oversight. A direct, cheap test using open models — no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Rahman et al. 2025 (arXiv:2506.02175) and Engels et al. 2025 (arXiv:2504.18530): debate beats consultancy under rough parity; Debate NSO 51.7% at Elo gap 400. Weak-honest-debater regime under-tested.

title: Does Representation Quality Predict Weak-to-Strong Generalization? A Probing Replication
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted test of a measurable property predicting safe supervisability.

original_idea.body:
# Does Representation Quality Predict Weak-to-Strong Generalization? A Probing Replication

**Problem:** An ICML 2025 result ('Representations Shape Weak-to-Strong Generalization') claims the strong model's representation structure predicts how much W2S generalization occurs. This is testable cheaply but has not been independently replicated on small open models with simple probes.

**Direction:** On a binary task, freeze several small open models. Measure each model's representation quality via linear-probe accuracy on ground-truth labels. Then run W2S: train a linear head on weak (small-model) labels and measure how much each strong model's head recovers ground truth. Correlate representation-quality with W2S recovery across models to test the predicted relationship.

**Why it matters:** If a simple, measurable representation property predicts when weak supervision elicits strong capability, overseers could pre-screen which models are safely supervisable. Frozen models + linear probes fit a consumer GPU; high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** ICML 2025 poster 'Representations Shape Weak-to-Strong Generalization' (icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/43511); builds on Burns et al. 2023 (arXiv:2312.09390) with open W2S code.

title: How Far Apart Can Overseer and Overseen Be Before Debate Collapses to Coin-Flip? Mapping the Elo-Gap Cliff
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped mapping of the tolerable capability gap that determines oversight scaling.

original_idea.body:
# How Far Apart Can Overseer and Overseen Be Before Debate Collapses to Coin-Flip? Mapping the Elo-Gap Cliff

**Problem:** Engels et al. (2025) report Debate NSO success of 51.7% at a general Elo gap of 400 — barely above chance. The shape of success-vs-Elo-gap near the cliff (gradual decline vs sudden collapse) is under-characterized and decides how much capability gap oversight can tolerate.

**Direction:** Using a small model ladder on a verifiable debate task, densely sample overseer-debater Elo gaps (via model-size and token-budget proxies) around the critical region. Fit the success-vs-gap curve and identify whether collapse is sharp (threshold) or smooth, and whether scaffolding (judge gets a checklist) shifts the cliff.

**Why it matters:** The tolerable capability gap is THE quantity that determines whether oversight scales to superhuman models. Independently mapping the cliff, and whether cheap scaffolding extends it, is high-value and runs as text rollouts on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Engels et al. 2025 (arXiv:2504.18530): Debate NSO 51.7% at Elo gap 400; oversight Elo piecewise-linear in capability with two plateaus.

title: Does the Persona Judge's Edge Come from Calibration, Not Accuracy? A Confidence-Decomposition Follow-Up
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted decomposition relevant to escalation in nested oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Does the Persona Judge's Edge Come from Calibration, Not Accuracy? A Confidence-Decomposition Follow-Up

**Problem:** Persona judges scored higher accuracy (Rahman et al. 2025), but accuracy alone hides whether they are better calibrated or just more decisive. For oversight, a judge that is accurate AND knows when it is unsure (flagging for escalation) is far more useful.

**Direction:** Re-score the released transcripts with persona vs default open judges, eliciting confidence per verdict. Compute calibration (ECE / reliability curves) and selective-accuracy (accuracy at high-confidence) for each judge type. Test whether personas improve calibration or merely shift the operating point.

**Why it matters:** Recursive/nested oversight depends on overseers knowing when to escalate. Decomposing the persona gain into accuracy vs calibration tells us whether personas make judges safer escalators or just more confident — directly relevant to systematic-error mitigation. Inference-only on public transcripts.

**Relevant context:** Rahman et al. 2025 (arXiv:2506.02175): persona judges 78.5% accuracy; calibration not reported. Calibration matters for escalation in nested oversight (Engels et al. 2025).

title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization on Code Correctness Labels
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted domain test of weak-to-strong elicitation for structured-reasoning oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Weak-to-Strong Generalization on Code Correctness Labels

**Problem:** OpenAI's weak-to-strong work and the EleutherAI replication tested W2S mostly on NLP classification (sentiment, NLI) and reward modeling. It is unclear whether the elicitation phenomenon holds when the 'hard' task is judging program correctness, a domain where weak supervisors make structured, systematic mistakes.

**Direction:** Take a small open model (e.g. Qwen1.5-0.5B) as the weak supervisor and a larger open model (e.g. Qwen1.5-7B) as the strong student, using the public openai/weak-to-strong codebase scaffolding. Generate weak labels for 'is this code correct' on a slice of HumanEval/MBPP-style problems (using public unit-test execution as ground truth), finetune the strong model on weak labels, and measure the performance gap recovered (PGR) versus the NLP-domain baseline.

**Why it matters:** Code correctness is a domain where ground truth is cheaply checkable, so it is an ideal external testbed for whether weak supervisors can elicit latent strong-model capability. If W2S degrades in code relative to NLP, it warns that the phenomenon does not transfer to structured reasoning domains that matter for superhuman oversight. Needs only open models and public datasets, no lab infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** Burns et al. 2023 (openai/weak-to-strong) found GPT-2-level supervisors recover most GPT-4 NLP performance but struggle on reward modeling and chess. EleutherAI replicated consistent W2S across 21 NLP datasets with Qwen1.5 and Llama 3. Code correctness with unit-test ground truth is an untested domain for the W2S elicitation framing.

title: Replicating the Auxiliary Confidence Loss Effect at Tiny Scale
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted replication testing brittleness of a key weak-to-strong oversight method.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating the Auxiliary Confidence Loss Effect at Tiny Scale

**Problem:** Burns et al. report that adding an auxiliary confidence loss dramatically improves weak-to-strong generalization, recovering near-GPT-3.5 performance from a GPT-2 supervisor. Whether this specific trick survives at the small open-model scale a beginner can run, and across model families, is unverified.

**Direction:** Reimplement the auxiliary confidence loss on top of the public W2S code using a tiny supervisor (GPT-2-small or Pythia-160M) and a modest student (Pythia-1.4B or Qwen1.5-1.8B). Run the standard W2S finetuning with and without the confidence loss on 3-4 NLP datasets, and report whether the PGR improvement replicates, fails, or reverses at this scale and on a non-GPT family.

**Why it matters:** The confidence loss is the headline 'simple method that helps' in the original paper. If it does not transfer to small or non-OpenAI models, practitioners building oversight tooling on open models may be relying on a brittle trick. A clean negative or positive replication is directly informative and fully achievable in 30h on a single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Burns et al. 2023: 'when finetuning GPT-4 with a GPT-2-level supervisor and an auxiliary confidence loss, they can recover close to GPT-3.5-level performance on NLP tasks.' Code is public at openai/weak-to-strong. The confidence loss is parameterized and easily ablated.

title: Debate vs Consultancy on a Non-Fiction Information-Asymmetry Task
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted domain test of debate's oversight advantage on technical text.

original_idea.body:
# Debate vs Consultancy on a Non-Fiction Information-Asymmetry Task

**Problem:** Kenton et al. (2024) showed debate beats consultancy when weak LLMs judge strong LLMs, but their information-asymmetry experiments centered on QuALITY fiction stories. It is unknown whether the debate advantage holds when the hidden information is dense technical/scientific text rather than a narrative.

**Direction:** Replicate the weak-judge debate-vs-consultancy comparison from Kenton et al. using a small open model as judge (e.g. Llama-3-8B) and a larger model as debater/consultant, but swap QuALITY for a non-fiction reading-comprehension set with hidden passages (e.g. a subset of a science/Wikipedia QA dataset where the judge does not see the passage). Measure judge accuracy under naive QA, consultancy, and debate, and compare the debate advantage magnitude to the fiction-domain baseline.

**Why it matters:** Real superhuman oversight will involve technical content, not stories. If debate's truth advantage shrinks on dense factual text, the protocol's practical value for scientific oversight is weaker than the QuALITY results suggest. Uses only open models and public QA data, classic counterfactual-value research.

**Relevant context:** Kenton et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.04622): debate consistently outperforms consultancy; debate beats direct QA under information asymmetry on QuALITY but results are mixed without asymmetry. The choice of fiction-based asymmetry is a fixed design decision ripe for a domain twist.

title: Easy-to-Hard Reward Model Generalization Outside Math
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted test of easy-to-hard evaluator generalization domain-specificity for oversight.

original_idea.body:
# Easy-to-Hard Reward Model Generalization Outside Math

**Problem:** Sun et al. (NeurIPS 2024) showed a reward model trained on easy MATH problems (levels 1-3) can score solutions to hard problems (levels 4-5). It is untested whether this easy-to-hard evaluator generalization holds in a non-math reasoning domain with its own easy/hard gradient.

**Direction:** Replicate the easy-to-hard evaluator idea on a domain with a natural difficulty grading, e.g. logical-deduction puzzles or graded reading-comprehension questions. Use a small open reward/scoring model trained (or few-shot prompted, to stay in 30h) on easy items, then measure its accuracy at ranking candidate answers to hard items, comparing the easy-trained evaluator to a hard-trained ceiling and an easy-only floor.

**Why it matters:** Easy-to-hard generalization is a core scalable-oversight hope: supervise on what humans can label, deploy on what they cannot. Knowing whether the MATH result is domain-specific or general is high-value and currently unknown. Can be scoped to few-shot scoring to avoid heavy training.

**Relevant context:** Sun et al. 2024 (arXiv:2403.09472): process-supervised reward models trained on easy problems effectively score hard problems; 7B RL model hit 34% on MATH500 using only easy supervision. The domain-specificity of this evaluator transfer is an open question explicitly flagged as a generation hint (easy-to-hard methods).
